newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Ivory Coast announces constitutional changes.
newsitem.headline: Ivory Coast announces constitutional changes.

text.p: The government of Ivory Coast is bringing in constitutional changes, including the establishment of a senate as a second parliamentary chamber, according to the minutes of a cabinet meeting published on Saturday.
The cabinet meeting, which was held on Friday, has also amended controversial electoral rules governing who is eligible to stand for the position of president.

The new text says that "any candidate for the Presidency of the Republic should be Ivorian by birth, born of an Ivorian father, and he will have to have resided in Ivory Coast in the 15 years after his birth, or in the 15 years preceding his candidacy".
Currently, both the father and mother of a candidate have to be Ivorian by birth, and the candidate must have lived in Ivory Coast during the five years before the election.

Former Prime Minister Alassane Ouattara was barred from standing in the last presidential election in 1995 because his father was not Ivorian, and because he was at the time working in Washington for the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
Opposition parties staged a boycott of the poll in protest.
The cabinet meeting agreed that the head of the future senate would, under the revised constitution, take over from the president if the latter could no longer carry out his duties.
If the senate head cannot assume responsibility for any reason, the oldest member of the government would take over.
"In either case, the person called upon to assume the interim position cannot be a candidate for the presidency," the statement said.
Currently it is the head of the National Assembly who is the first in line if the president dies or is otherwise unable to govern, and he or she can see out the end of the mandate.
Current President Henri Konan Bedie benefited from this clause when he took over after the death of long-time president Felix Houphouet-Boigny in December 1993.
The revised constitution will be put before parliament when it reassembles in October.
It is certain to be adopted, since the ruling PDCI party, which has been in power since independence from France in 1960, has 149 of the 175 seats.
